questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has had epigastric discomfort, nausea and two vomits for 90 minutes. She is clammy. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. ECG (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Older women and people with diabetes often present atypically, without chest pain; ST elevation in V1–V4 is an anterior (LAD) STEMI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: Her abdomen is soft and non-tender
steps.x: Atypical symptoms in an older diabetic woman with a soft abdomen.

elim: Would cause epigastric tenderness and does not cause regional ST elevation.
Right upper quadrant pain; ECG would be normal.
Does not cause sweating or ST elevation.
The abdomen would be rigid and tender.

steps.x: **B. Anterior ST elevation myocardial infarction.** Diabetics and women can present without chest pain: always do the ECG.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has had central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm for 50 minutes. He smokes and has hypercholesterolaemia. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal inferior depression.

questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: ST elevation in the lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 points to the left circumflex artery.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm
steps.x: Classic ischaemic pain; now read which leads are elevated.

elim: Would give ST elevation in V1–V4 (anterior).
Usually widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR and shock.
Supplies the inferior wall; would give changes in II, III and aVF.
Gives ST elevation in II, III and aVF (inferior).

steps.x: **B. Left circumflex artery.** II, III, aVF = RCA; V1–V4 = LAD; I, aVL (V5–V6) = circumflex.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had central chest pain, sweating and nausea for 1 hour. He felt faint on standing. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 54 bpm, BP 108/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. ECG (see item resources); it also shows left axis deviation.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL, plus bradycardia, is an inferior (RCA) STEMI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Ischaemic pain with bradycardia: think RCA and the inferior leads.

elim: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression, no reciprocal change.
Would show ST elevation in V1–V4.
Would show ST elevation in I and aVL, which are depressed here.
There is ST elevation.

steps.x: **C. Inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction.** Inferior STEMI = II, III, aVF + reciprocal I/aVL; often bradycardic.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has had central chest heaviness with sweating for 4 hours, now easing. He has hypertension and smokes. There is no chest wall tenderness and the pain does not change with breathing. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. Troponin is raised and rises further at 3 hours. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST depression V4–V6 with T wave inversion in I and aVL.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ischaemic pain with ST depression/T wave inversion and a rising troponin is an NSTEMI; unstable angina has a normal troponin.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: Troponin is raised and rises further
steps.x: Ischaemic ECG changes without ST elevation, plus a rising troponin.

elim: Causes chest wall tenderness and pain on inspiration, with a normal troponin.
There is no ST elevation.
Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest; troponin is normal.
Same ECG changes possible, but the troponin is normal.

steps.x: **B. Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.** NSTEMI = no ST elevation + raised troponin. Unstable angina = normal troponin.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has had angina on climbing two flights of stairs for a year. Over the past 10 days the pain has come on after walking 20 metres and is happening several times a day, relieved by rest and GTN. She is pain free now. Her ECG shows T wave inversion in V4–V6. Troponin at 0 and 3 hours is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Crescendo angina (increasing frequency, less exertion) with ischaemic ECG changes but normal serial troponins is unstable angina.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: Troponin at 0 and 3 hours is normal
steps.x: A previously stable pattern now accelerating; troponin negative.

elim: Troponin would be raised.
Pain at rest from vasospasm, often with transient ST elevation.
No ST elevation and troponin is normal.
Pain was stable for a year but is now crescendo, so no longer stable.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Crescendo angina + normal troponin = unstable angina (an ACS, not stable angina).

questions.stem: A 69 year old man is 6 hours after a large anterior STEMI. He is confused and breathless. His hands are cold and clammy. His temperature is 36.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. There are coarse crackles to both mid zones. Urine output is 10 mL/hour.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hypotension, poor perfusion and lung crackles after a large MI is cardiogenic shock; crackles are a poor prognostic sign.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: coarse crackles to both mid zones
steps.x: Pump failure after a large infarct.

elim: Raised JVP with clear lungs and muffled heart sounds, not pulmonary crackles.
No fluid or blood loss, and lungs would be clear.
Would not cause widespread crackles.
Afebrile with cold peripheries; no source of infection.

steps.x: **B. Cardiogenic shock.** Post-MI hypotension + crackles = cardiogenic shock (poor prognosis).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is in the coronary care unit 2 hours after primary PCI for an inferior STEMI. He suddenly becomes unresponsive. He has no pulse and is not breathing. The cardiac monitor rhythm strip is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Monitor rhythm strip
visual.caption: Chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable QRS complexes.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: Chaotic activity with no QRS complexes is ventricular fibrillation, the commonest cause of death in ACS, arising from electrically unstable ischaemic or reperfused myocardium.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Cardiac arrest soon after reperfusion.

elim: Would be a flat line.
Irregular narrow QRS complexes with a pulse.
Regular slow QRS complexes dissociated from P waves.
Regular, broad, uniform complexes.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular fibrillation.** VF is the commonest cause of death in ACS: shockable, defibrillate.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has had central crushing chest pain with sweating for 40 minutes. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has a strong family history of heart disease. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation V1–V6, I and aVL: anterolateral.

questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: Anterior (V1–V4) plus lateral (V5–V6, I, aVL) ST elevation is an anterolateral STEMI from a proximal LAD occlusion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: central crushing chest pain with sweating
strong family history of heart disease
steps.x: Classic ischaemic pain in a high-risk patient.

elim: Gives inferior ST elevation.
Gives lateral changes only, without V1–V3 elevation.
Gives posterior or inferior changes.
Supplies the right ventricle; would not cause anterolateral ST elevation.

steps.x: **D. Proximal left anterior descending artery.** V1–V3 = anterior (LAD); add V5–V6 = anterolateral.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has had central chest tightness at rest for 2 hours. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He is now pain free. Examination is normal. His ECG is normal. Serial high-sensitivity troponin is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An NSTEMI can have a normal ECG; a rising troponin confirms infarction, distinguishing it from unstable angina.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Rest pain, normal ECG, rising troponin.

elim: Pleuritic, positional pain with widespread ST elevation.
Exertional pain with a normal troponin.
Usually after emotional stress with ECG changes; not the most likely here.
Troponin would be normal.

steps.x: **B. Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.** Normal ECG does not exclude NSTEMI: look for a rising troponin.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman is 4 days after an anterior STEMI. She suddenly becomes breathless and hypotensive. Her pulse rate is 114 bpm, BP 88/56 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. There are bibasal crackles. She had a normal heart examination on admission.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of her heart?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex
New loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge
questions.e: Ventricular septal rupture a few days after MI causes a new pansystolic murmur with acute heart failure; it needs urgent echo and surgical repair.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Sudden heart failure days after MI: a mechanical complication.

elim: Aortic regurgitation; not a typical post-MI mechanical complication.
Aortic stenosis, which is chronic.
Mitral stenosis, which is chronic.
Pericarditis does not cause sudden heart failure and shock.

steps.x: **D. New loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge.** Days after MI + sudden heart failure + new pansystolic murmur = septal (or papillary) rupture.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had an MI treated with PCI 3 weeks ago. He now has sharp central chest pain that is better sitting forward, with a low-grade fever. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. A pericardial friction rub is heard. An ECG is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
o: Deep Q waves only in V1–V4
Regional ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal changes
Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression
questions.e: Dressler's syndrome (post-infarction pericarditis) gives widespread ST elevation with PR depression, not regional changes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Weeks after MI: pericarditis.

elim: Old infarct; does not explain new pleuritic pain and rub.
Hyperkalaemia.
A new inferior STEMI, not pericarditis.
A rarely seen sign of pulmonary embolism.

steps.x: **E. Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.** Dressler's: weeks post-MI, pleuritic positional pain, fever, widespread ST elevation + PR depression.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is admitted with an inferior STEMI from a proximal right coronary artery occlusion and is awaiting PCI. Over 10 minutes he becomes dizzy and grey. His pulse rate is 34 bpm and BP 80/48 mmHg. A rhythm strip is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Lead II rhythm strip
visual.caption: P waves march through at a regular rate unrelated to slow, regular QRS complexes.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: Proximal RCA occlusion supplies the AV node, so inferior STEMI carries a high risk of complete heart block, with P waves and QRS complexes dissociated.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Inferior MI with profound bradycardia and hypotension.

elim: A long PR interval but every P wave is conducted; rate is normal.
PR lengthens progressively until a beat is dropped.
Fixed PR with intermittently dropped beats.
Every P wave is followed by a QRS.

steps.x: **A. Complete heart block.** Inferior (RCA) STEMI: watch for complete heart block; urgent PCI.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had central crushing chest pain with sweating for 45 minutes. He smokes. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 144/88 mmHg. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V2–V5. A high-sensitivity troponin taken on arrival is within the normal range.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ST elevation with typical pain is a STEMI; troponin is released only from dead myocytes and may not rise for 2–3 hours, so a normal early result does not exclude it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Very early presentation with ST elevation.

elim: Widespread, not regional, ST elevation, with pleuritic pain.
There is ST elevation.
Pain at rest for 45 minutes with ST elevation is not stable angina.
ST elevation means infarction; an early troponin may not have risen yet.

steps.x: **C. ST elevation myocardial infarction.** STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG; never wait for troponin.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with type 2 diabetes fainted at home while making tea. She now feels sick and breathless but has no chest pain. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her heart sounds are normal. ECG shows ST depression in V3–V6. Troponin is raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Older diabetic women may present with syncope, nausea or breathlessness rather than chest pain; ST depression with raised troponin is an NSTEMI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Atypical presentation, ischaemic ECG, raised troponin.

elim: Exertional syncope with an ejection systolic murmur; her heart sounds are normal.
Would not cause ischaemic ECG changes and a raised troponin.
Troponin is raised, so this is infarction.
A benign faint does not raise troponin.

steps.x: **B. Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.** Syncope, breathlessness or nausea in older diabetics may be ACS.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man walks into the Emergency Department with 30 minutes of central chest pain radiating to his jaw. He is sweaty and nauseated. He has hypertension. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 150/92 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A 12-lead ECG should be done within 10 minutes of arrival to identify STEMI, which needs immediate reperfusion.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: central chest pain radiating to his jaw
steps.x: Typical ischaemic chest pain on arrival.

elim: Done, but after the ECG.
For stable chest pain, not an acute presentation.
Dangerous in a possible ACS.
Needed, but the ECG within 10 minutes decides on reperfusion.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** Suspected ACS: ECG within 10 minutes.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has an NSTEMI confirmed by a rising troponin and ST depression in V4–V6. She has been given aspirin 300 mg. She is now pain free and haemodynamically stable. The team must decide whether she needs early coronary angiography.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tool to guide this decision?
questions.e: The GRACE score risk-stratifies NSTEMI and decides whether angiography is needed within 72 hours.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: decide whether she needs early coronary angiography
steps.x: Risk stratifying an NSTEMI.

elim: Estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
Assesses pneumonia severity.
Estimates bleeding risk on anticoagulation.
Estimates the probability of DVT or PE.

steps.x: **C. GRACE score.** NSTEMI: aspirin 300 mg + calculate GRACE.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is 5 days after an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI. He develops sudden breathlessness. His pulse rate is 116 bpm, BP 90/58 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There is a new loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge and bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: A new pansystolic murmur with acute heart failure after MI suggests ventricular septal rupture; urgent echo confirms it before surgical repair.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Suspected ventricular septal rupture.

elim: The murmur points to a mechanical cardiac complication, not PE.
Dangerous and unhelpful in acute heart failure.
Will be raised from the recent MI and does not show the defect.
Confirms heart failure but not its cause.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** Post-MI new murmur + heart failure: urgent echocardiogram.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has an NSTEMI and is to start fondaparinux while awaiting angiography. She has had an ECG and troponin. She takes ramipril and furosemide for heart failure. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test to check before starting fondaparinux?
questions.e: Other initial tests in ACS are FBC, U&Es and chest X-ray; fondaparinux is renally cleared, so renal function must be checked first.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
A renally cleared anticoagulant in a patient on diuretics and an ACE inhibitor.

elim: Not relevant to anticoagulant safety.
Long-term glucose control; not needed before anticoagulation.
Guides secondary prevention, not anticoagulant safety.
Not needed before fondaparinux.

steps.x: **E. Urea and electrolytes.** ACS baseline tests: FBC, U&Es, chest X-ray.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with an inferior STEMI is at a rural hospital 3 hours from a PCI centre. Symptoms began 2 hours ago. He has been given fondaparinux and alteplase. His BP is 134/82 mmHg and he still has some chest pain.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Exercise tolerance test the next day
questions.e: After fibrinolysis, repeat the ECG at 60–90 minutes; persistent ST elevation means failed reperfusion and the need for urgent PCI.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Fibrinolysis given; you must check whether it worked.

elim: Does not guide acute management after fibrinolysis.
Does not tell you if reperfusion has worked.
Contraindicated in an acute MI.
Too slow to decide on rescue PCI.

steps.x: **D. Repeat ECG 60–90 minutes after fibrinolysis.** Post-fibrinolysis: repeat ECG at 60–90 min; persisting ST elevation → urgent PCI.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman has had central crushing chest pain with sweating for 1 hour. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her 12-lead ECG shows horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves in V1 and V2. There is no ST elevation in the standard leads.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation; posterior leads V7–V9 show the ST elevation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: tall R waves in V1 and V2
steps.x: Reciprocal change in the anterior leads.

elim: Will not show the infarct.
No features of dissection, such as tearing back pain or unequal pulses.
Dangerous in a suspected ACS.
Delays reperfusion of a possible posterior STEMI.

steps.x: **D. Posterior lead ECG (V7–V9).** Posterior MI: ST elevation V7–V9 with reciprocal V1–V3 depression.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man had 20 minutes of central chest pain at rest this morning. He is now pain free. He has hypertension and smokes. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. His ECG shows T wave inversion in V4–V6. His first troponin, taken 1 hour after the pain began, is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish unstable angina from NSTEMI?
questions.e: Troponin does not rise until 2–3 hours after MI, so a repeat sample shows whether it is rising (NSTEMI) or stays normal (unstable angina).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: taken 1 hour after the pain began
steps.x: Ischaemic ECG changes; troponin taken too early.

elim: Does not detect myocardial necrosis.
Shows coronary anatomy but not infarction.
Used for suspected VTE.
Unsafe in a suspected ACS and does not detect infarction.

steps.x: **E. Repeat high-sensitivity troponin.** Diagnosis = clinical + ECG + troponin. Serial troponins: rise = NSTEMI, normal = unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has had central chest pain radiating to his left arm for 1 hour. His ECG shows T wave inversion in V4–V6 and his first troponin is awaited. He has no allergies and no history of bleeding. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Aspirin 300 mg is given immediately in suspected ACS, before the diagnosis is confirmed.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Suspected ACS, not yet confirmed.

elim: Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI when PCI cannot be delivered in time.
Secondary prevention, not the first acute drug.
A maintenance dose; the second antiplatelet comes after aspirin and risk assessment.
Secondary prevention started within 24 hours, not the first drug.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin 300 mg orally.** Suspected ACS: aspirin 300 mg now, don't wait for troponin.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with an inferior STEMI is being prepared for primary PCI. He has had aspirin 300 mg. He has severe chest pain, 8 out of 10. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 58 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step for his pain?
questions.e: Severe ACS pain is treated with IV morphine plus an antiemetic; GTN is avoided when systolic BP is below 90 mmHg and oxygen is only given if saturations are below 94%.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Hypotensive and not hypoxic, with severe pain.

elim: Not needed with saturations of 97%; oxygen only if below 94%.
Nitrates are avoided with systolic BP below 90 mmHg.
NSAIDs are avoided in ACS and will not control severe pain.
Nitrates are avoided with systolic BP below 90 mmHg.

steps.x: **C. IV morphine with metoclopramide.** MONA with rules: O2 only if <94%, no GTN if SBP <90, morphine + antiemetic.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has an anterior STEMI and is going straight to the catheter lab for primary PCI. He has had aspirin 300 mg. He takes no regular medicines and is not anticoagulated. He has no history of stroke or bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate second antiplatelet drug to give now?
questions.e: Prasugrel is the second antiplatelet for patients going for PCI who are not anticoagulated; clopidogrel is used if they already take an anticoagulant.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: going straight to the catheter lab
steps.x: PCI planned, no anticoagulant.

elim: An anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet.
Reserved for patients already on an anticoagulant.
Used in stroke prevention, not ACS.
An anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet.

steps.x: **D. Prasugrel.** Second antiplatelet: prasugrel (PCI, not anticoagulated); clopidogrel if anticoagulated.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has an NSTEMI. Her GRACE score is 5.4% and angiography is planned in 48 hours. She has had aspirin and ticagrelor. Her eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73m². She has no bleeding history. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg, and she is pain free.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant while she awaits angiography?
questions.e: Fondaparinux is the first-line anticoagulant in ACS when PCI is not immediate; unfractionated heparin is the alternative.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Not immediate PCI; renal function adequate.

elim: A direct oral anticoagulant, not used for acute ACS anticoagulation.
Not used in acute ACS.
Not the acute ACS anticoagulant.
Slow onset; not used in acute ACS.

steps.x: **C. Fondaparinux.** ACS anticoagulation: fondaparinux first-line pending angiography (heparin alternative).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has an inferior STEMI at a district hospital. Symptoms began 3 hours ago. The nearest PCI centre cannot take him for 3 hours. His BP is 196/118 mmHg despite IV GTN and morphine. He has no other contraindications.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Primary PCI is preferred within 120 minutes; otherwise fibrinolysis, but severe hypertension contraindicates it, so he should be transferred for PCI.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
PCI delayed, but fibrinolysis contraindicated.

elim: Severe uncontrolled hypertension (above 180/110) contraindicates fibrinolysis.
A STEMI needs reperfusion.
This is the NSTEMI pathway, not STEMI.
Also a fibrinolytic and also contraindicated.

steps.x: **E. Transfer for primary PCI.** STEMI: PPCI if deliverable within 120 min, otherwise fibrinolysis unless contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with an anterior STEMI was given fondaparinux and alteplase at a hospital without PCI facilities. A repeat ECG 90 minutes later shows persistent ST elevation in V1–V4 with ongoing chest pain. Her BP is 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent ST elevation 60–90 minutes after fibrinolysis means failed reperfusion; she needs urgent rescue PCI.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: 90 minutes later shows persistent ST elevation
steps.x: Failed fibrinolysis.

elim: Not the immediate reperfusion step after failed fibrinolysis.
Repeat fibrinolysis is not recommended.
Delays reperfusion of a failing infarct.
Does not reopen the artery.

steps.x: **D. Rescue PCI.** Persistent ST elevation after fibrinolysis: urgent PCI.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had central crushing chest pain with sweating for 1 hour. His ECG shows left bundle branch block. An ECG from a clinic visit 4 months ago showed normal conduction. His BP is 132/80 mmHg. The PCI centre is 20 minutes away. He has had aspirin 300 mg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: New left bundle branch block with ischaemic pain is treated as a STEMI; primary PCI is first line if it can be delivered within 120 minutes.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
New LBBB = STEMI equivalent; PCI close by.

elim: The NSTEMI pathway; new LBBB is treated as STEMI.
Dangerous in ACS.
PCI can be delivered well within 120 minutes.
Delays reperfusion.

steps.x: **D. Primary PCI.** New LBBB with ACS symptoms: manage as STEMI.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes had an NSTEMI and underwent coronary angiography. It shows severe stenoses in the left anterior descending, left circumflex and right coronary arteries. He is now pain free and stable on dual antiplatelet therapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Single stent to the right coronary artery
questions.e: CABG is considered for left main stem disease, triple vessel disease or patients unsuitable for PCI.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: left anterior descending, left circumflex and right coronary arteries
steps.x: Triple vessel disease in a diabetic patient.

elim: For STEMI when PCI is unavailable, not for stable triple vessel disease.
Increases bleeding without revascularising.
Undertreats triple vessel disease.
Leaves two diseased vessels untreated.

steps.x: **A. Coronary artery bypass grafting.** CABG: left main, triple vessel disease, unsuitable for PCI, or ongoing instability after PCI.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has an NSTEMI. She has had aspirin 300 mg. Her GRACE score is 1.9%. She is pain free and stable, with a pulse rate of 74 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. She is not anticoagulated, has no history of bleeding and a normal platelet count.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional antiplatelet?
questions.e: With a GRACE score of 3% or less, add a second antiplatelet: ticagrelor, or clopidogrel 300 mg if bleeding risk is high.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Low-risk NSTEMI without bleeding risk.

elim: A fibrinolytic, not used for NSTEMI.
Used if bleeding risk is high; she has none.
Not used in ACS.
Given when going for PCI, which is not planned here.

steps.x: **E. Ticagrelor.** NSTEMI GRACE ≤3%: ticagrelor (clopidogrel if high bleeding risk).

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is being discharged 4 days after an inferior STEMI treated with primary PCI. His ejection fraction is 55%. He takes aspirin 75 mg, ticagrelor, ramipril and bisoprolol. His total cholesterol is 5.6 mmol/L. He has no muscle problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate lipid-lowering treatment?
questions.e: Secondary prevention after MI is ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, high-dose atorvastatin 80 mg and lifelong aspirin, with the second antiplatelet for 12 months.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: aspirin 75 mg, ticagrelor, ramipril and bisoprolol
steps.x: Already on the other secondary prevention drugs.

elim: The primary prevention dose, not post-MI.
Not first line; a high-intensity statin comes first.
Low intensity.
Low intensity.
